cells.tense: Your hands are in the work right now and the work is holding.
cells.act: do the giving in the open this time, where it was always done unseen
cells.ask: Pick one piece of this care and do it where the person it serves can watch. One sitting, with them there. Let them see your hands at it, and when it's finished, say nothing.
cells.core:
You're tending something that grows — a person, a household, a shared thing — and your hands are in it. You can feel when it needs less and when it needs more, and you move the water without thinking twice. That's attention with a spine. What stays alive does so because you keep showing up for it.

Much of that happens off to the side, and quiet is fine. Still, one piece of it could be done where the person it serves is watching, with them there while you work. You finish, you set it down. The point isn't thanks. It's that the thing you hand over gets seen by the one receiving it, and not only carried by you.
cells.sheetLine: Let one piece of the care be watched.
cells.verb: tending what grows, by hand, through the years
cells.place: beside someone, aligned, feeling with them and not only about them

cells.tense: The person you're tending is fine where they are, and you're already braced over a future they haven't reached.
cells.act: let the satisfaction of a finished thing land
cells.ask: Go stand in something you already finished helping — a problem solved, a season done. Stay an hour and improve nothing, with no next problem lined up behind it.
cells.core:
You tend something real, and your hands are strong at it. They run past the thing itself. The person you care for is a step behind where your head has already placed them, and you're packing for a trip they haven't booked. You reach past what's here because the future got early in you. Care running hot like that can leave you in a garden that is finished enough, planning the next row.

So let a finished thing land. Go back to what you already helped reach solid ground and stand in it for an hour — no fixing, no next problem. Not a reward, and not a lesson. A gardener who doesn't walk their garden is just maintenance with legs. Walk it once, keep your hands off the beds, and the caring returns as something other than a job.
cells.sheetLine: The garden is done enough. Walk it, hands off.

cells.tense: The work is still going, but part of you keeps standing at a way in you already passed.
cells.act: keep following the star after everything that has happened
cells.ask: Stay with what you already chose — the person, the thing you're growing — expecting no sign it's working. Call, water it, or do the next plain piece. No clock on it.
cells.core:
You tend something, and your hands still know the steps even when the rest of you is somewhere back down the way you came. You watch from a threshold while your hands keep up the work — not quit, not fully arrived. The caring carries on with you only partly in it.

What returns your weight is staying with what you already chose. Not a new promise; the old one, kept small. Call the person. Water the thing. Do the next plain piece without waiting for proof it's landing. Your feet come back under you that way. Nothing from before needs repairing — you're stepping through a way in that's already open.
cells.sheetLine: Stay with what you chose. No proof needed.

cells.tense: Quiet care is holding this, and your account of it is that the two of you simply fit.
cells.act: accept the acknowledgment when it comes
cells.ask: Next time someone thanks you for what you did for them, don't wave it off. Take it — "you're welcome," and stop there. Don't hand it back.
cells.core:
You keep something alive with steady hands — a person, a long thing you care about — and it holds partly because you keep showing up. That's real. What you don't count is your part in it. When someone thanks you, you point at the two of you getting along, as though the warmth between you were something that simply happens rather than something your hands keep making.

So take one thank-you and own it out loud. The next small one, the real one — don't hand it away. "You're welcome" is the whole act, three words. Whether it feels awkward or easy afterward doesn't matter. No speech, no explanation. Let the work carry your name once, out where it can be heard, and see how that sits.
cells.sheetLine: Take the next thank-you. It has your name on it.
